transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-06
Start time: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Marissa Chen (Redwood SE), Liam O'Neal (Redwood Product), Maya Gonzalez (Hearthline Head of ML), Derek Shaw (Hearthline Platform Eng), Priya Menon (Hearthline Data Privacy), Alex Kim (Hearthline PM)

Summary (auto):
Quick EvalOps / quality-monitoring demo focused on prompt sets, regression alerts, and A/B split comparisons. Customer concerned about data residency, SOC2, and how Redwood handles private prompts and KV cache. Discussed pilot plan and next steps for a 1-week benchmarking run.

Topics covered (auto):
- Prompt-set creation and grouping
- Regression alert configuration and thresholds
- A/B split setup and sample analysis
- API vs Console workflows for rapid iteration
- Security / data residency concerns and SOC2 questions

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Jordan Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Uh, we'll kick off — um — quick intros. I'm Jordan, AE on the Redwood Inference team.
[00:08] Maya Gonzalez: Hi, Maya here. Head of ML at Hearthline.
[00:11] Derek Shaw: Derek, platform.
[00:14] Priya Menon: Priya, data privacy.
[00:16] Alex Kim: Alex, PM.
[00:18] Marissa Chen: Marissa, solutions engineering. Liam's on for product context.
[00:22] Liam O'Neal: Hey all.
[00:24] Jordan Patel: Cool. Quick agenda — we'll show a short console walkthrough for EvalOps Lite, then jump to API examples for running A/B splits, then cover regression alerts and how you can tie them to prompt-sets. Leave time for Q&A and next steps. Sound okay?
[00:36] Maya Gonzalez: Yep, sounds good. The key thing for us is: the retail chat assistant is regressing occasionally when we update the model, so we need signal and automated alerts. Also curious about how you guys define prompt-sets and do traffic splits.
[00:50] Jordan Patel: Great. Marissa, do you want to share the screen and start in the console?
[00:55] Marissa Chen: Yep, sharing now. Can you all see the Redwood console? There's a bit of lag, let me know.
[01:03] Alex Kim: Looks good, I see the dashboard.
[01:06] Marissa Chen: Okay, starting in the EvalOps tab — we keep a lightweight mode called EvalOps Lite which is designed for teams that want quick guardrails without a heavy eval infra. First thing: prompt-set groups. You can create groups for "Checkout flow", "Returns flow", and so on. I'm opening our Hearthline starter pack — you'll see examples from your sample templates.
[01:28] Marissa Chen: The prompt set shows the original user query, a canonical expected answer, and a couple of labels we use to measure correctness, safety, and policy. We support custom metrics — you can upload the heuristics or label sets from your QA team.
[01:42] Maya Gonzalez: When you say "canonical expected answer" is that free text, or do you need structured JSON for scoring?
[01:47] Marissa Chen: Both. You can do free-text fuzzy matching, exact match, or structured extraction match — e.g., we support JSON path extraction so you can assert that an order_id is present and in the right format. We also have pairwise comparison scoring for A/B comparisons.
[02:01] Derek Shaw: Pairwise — does that compare token-by-token or semantic similarity?
[02:05] Marissa Chen: It's configurable. The default is semantic similarity using embeddings plus an optional ngram overlap. We tried to keep it flexible because different customers want different benchmarks.
[02:16] Jordan Patel: Quick aside — on the backend we call out to our embeddings catalog; you can use a hosted embedding model or bring your own. For private deployments, you can keep embeddings in your VPC.
[02:27] Priya Menon: That brings up an important point: data retention and keys. How long do you store prompts and outputs? Are they encrypted with customer-managed keys?
[02:36] Marissa Chen: Defaults are 30 days for EvalOps Lite, but for Dedicated or Private you can set retention policies and use customer-managed KMS/HSM. Also, audit logs are available for compliance. We'll send the SOC2 and KMS docs after.
[02:50] Maya Gonzalez: Perfect.
[02:53] Marissa Chen: Back to the demo — here's an example A/B split. I'm creating a split: Variant A uses the standard tuned model we recommend, Variant B is a quantized variant for cost savings. You can set traffic weights and define the prompt-set you'll use to evaluate. We often run a rolling window test (e.g., last 7 days) or a static sample.
[03:12] Marissa Chen: We also show a visual of the pairwise comparisons — each row is a prompt, and columns show Variant A/B outputs with a suggested winner. There's a threshold slider that determines when an automated regression alert fires.
[03:24] Alex Kim: So the slider — is that sliding on a delta of the pairwise score, or an absolute metric like pass rate drop?
[03:30] Marissa Chen: You choose. You can set it to trigger if Variant B's pass rate is X percentage points below A over the last N prompts, or if the semantic similarity delta exceeds a threshold.
[03:41] Maya Gonzalez: And when an alert fires, what's the notification path? Slack? Email? Pager?
[03:45] Marissa Chen: We support Slack, webhook, email, and we can plug into Opsgenie/PagerDuty through webhooks. You can also tie alerts to a canary rollback policy so production traffic flips back to the safe model automatically.
[03:58] Derek Shaw: Canary rollback — does that work with Dedicated capacity where we've reserved instances?
[04:03] Jordan Patel: Yes, the traffic routing layer handles model variants regardless of hosting mode. If Dedicated is out of capacity for the fallback model we can route to a compatible hosted variant. There are configurable fallbacks.
[04:14] Priya Menon: Does routing leak any metadata? For example, if we route to hosted fallback, does Redwood see the raw prompts? We need to be explicit for compliance.
[04:23] Marissa Chen: Short answer: by default hosted routes pass prompts through Redwood's processing pipeline, but for Private deployments you can enable an end-to-end private path. We'll include exact data flow diagrams in the security pack.
[04:35] Maya Gonzalez: Good. Can we dive into the API flow? We want automated A/B runs from our pipeline.
[04:40] Jordan Patel: Sure — Marissa, can you switch to the API tab?
[04:44] Marissa Chen: On it. So you can hit /v1/eval/run with a payload that contains the prompt-set id, variants config, and evaluation config. Example payloads are in the SDK. I'll paste one in the chat.
[04:56] Marissa Chen (chat): [link] https://redwood.ai/docs/examples/eval-api-payloads (note: link is illustrative)
[05:03] Maya Gonzalez: The API looks straightforward. For high throughput tests, do you recommend batching?
[05:08] Marissa Chen: Yes, we have recommended batch sizes per model and sequence length. For the eval runs, you can do continuous batching — Redwood's runtime will optimize kernels and KV cache to avoid repeated prefix costs. That said, if you want token-accurate latency numbers you should benchmark with the same batching profile as production.
[05:26] Derek Shaw: Any gotchas around KV cache and A/B? If Variant B uses a different model that isn't compatible with the KV format, do you rewarm caches?
[05:34] Marissa Chen: Great question. We try to route only to compatible variants for KV reuse; when that's not possible we rewarm, and we surface the additional latency cost in the dashboard. There's a flag to prefer latency over cost which will pick variants to avoid rewarm.
[05:48] Liam O'Neal: Also worth noting the per-token cost breakdown in the console — you can see body tokens vs prompt tokens, caching hits, and per-model unit cost so you can optimize the economics during A/B tests.
[05:59] Maya Gonzalez: That cost breakdown is useful. For our stakeholders, we need reporting to show ROI — like "cost per resolution". Can we compute custom metrics?
[06:07] Marissa Chen: Yes, you can define custom composed metrics. For example, cost per resolution = (model_cost + infra_charge) / number_of_successful_resolutions. You can send external signals back into EvalOps via webhooks to enrich the evaluation.
[06:20] Priya Menon: On the legal side, do you maintain a data processing agreement and model risk agreement? We need to see that for procurement.
[06:26] Jordan Patel: Yes, we have standard DPA and can add clauses for data residency in enterprise contracts. We'll loop legal in next step.
[06:33] Maya Gonzalez: Can we walk through a concrete regression alert example?
[06:36] Marissa Chen: Sure — I have a sample. We had a case where an upgrade caused order confirmation IDs to be malformed in 3% of responses. We set a regression alert: metric = structured extraction pass rate for order_id, window = 48 hours, threshold = drop of more than 1.5 percentage points. When that fired we got a Slack alert with an example prompt + two variant responses. The AE then triggered a canary rollback.
[06:58] Derek Shaw: How are examples selected in the alert? Random sample, hardest failures, or deterministic?
[07:03] Marissa Chen: You can choose. Default is selected by highest semantic distance from expected answer and frequency. There's also a reproducible sample id so you can replay the exact prompt through the API.
[07:14] Alex Kim: Replayable sample IDs — nice. That helps debugging.
[07:18] Maya Gonzalez: What about false positives? Our customer success team doesn't want noisy alerts.
[07:23] Marissa Chen: We offer multiple levers — smoothing over windows, minimum sample counts, and an adjustable confidence threshold on the pairwise scorer. You can also exclude known flaky prompts by tag.
[07:34] Priya Menon: For auditability we need full logs of what triggered the alert — prompt, variants, timestamps, and the computed scores. Does Redwood keep that?
[07:43] Marissa Chen: Yes, those artifacts are stored and can be exported. For private deployments you can opt to store them in your internal S3.
[07:51] Jordan Patel: Quick note on SKU — EvalOps Lite is included in our standard hosted plan; advanced retention and private S3 exports are part of Dedicated/Private add-ons. We'll share pricing in the follow-up.
[08:03] Maya Gonzalez: Can you show an example A/B comparison report?
[08:07] Marissa Chen: Switching to the AB report... here we have a waterfall view. Top of the report shows pass rates by metric, then a per-prompt table with pairwise judgment and suggested winner, finally a statistical summary (p-values and confidence intervals; you can set whether to use bootstrap or asymptotic tests).
[08:27] Derek Shaw: Are the tests customizable? We tend to prefer non-parametric tests for our skewed traffic distributions.
[08:33] Marissa Chen: Yes, you can pick from a list — chi-squared, bootstrap resampling, Mann-Whitney U, etc.
[08:39] Maya Gonzalez: Can I attach business metrics to the split? Like conversions or downstream revenue?
[08:43] Marissa Chen: Absolutely. There's a "business-signal" attachment where you can paste your downstream KPI, and when you run the A/B it will compute both eval metrics and your business metric delta.
[08:53] Alex Kim: Does Redwood pull that automatically from our production analytics or do we push it?
[08:57] Marissa Chen: Both. You can push via API or connect a read-only view of your analytics to automatically ingest conversion events. For security-sensitive shops you typically push a hashed signal.
[09:08] Maya Gonzalez: Good. Two more things — first, latency SLOs. We need guaranteed p95 under 250ms for short responses under Dedicated. Can you meet that?
[09:17] Jordan Patel: Our Dedicated SLAs can be configured for p95 targets; the exact number depends on model and sequence length. For short sequences with optimized kernels we've hit p95 ~180ms in customers similar to your traffic profiles. We'll propose an SLA in the quote.
[09:31] Priya Menon: If we sign Dedicated, can we keep keys in our KMS and use a private control plane?
[09:36] Jordan Patel: Yes, Private control plane is an option — keys in your KMS, VPC peering or private link for the control plane, and audit logs forwarded to your SIEM.
[09:45] Maya Gonzalez: Last topic: data used for evals — do you have redaction or PII filters built-in? We can't send raw customer emails.
[09:52] Marissa Chen: We have PII redaction heuristics and integrations with Data Loss Prevention pipelines. For the pilot we recommend providing a de-identified sample or using our local redaction preprocessor in the SDK.
[10:04] Derek Shaw: Sounds reasonable.
[10:07] Jordan Patel: Okay, quick recap and concrete next steps: Jordan will send SOC2 and security pack, Marissa to share pilot plan and prompt-set template, Hearthline to prepare a 5k-sample of de-identified prompts, and we'll aim to kick off a 1-week benchmark on Dedicated the week of 8/19. Any objections?
[10:26] Maya Gonzalez: No objections. One ask — can you include an example contract clause for data residency?
[10:31] Jordan Patel: Yes. We'll add that to the legal package.
[10:34] Priya Menon: Also please include the KMS integration steps so our infra team can estimate work.
[10:39] Jordan Patel: Will do.
[10:41] Alex Kim: And one small ask — can you add an example of an alert payload so our engineers can wire the webhook quickly?
[10:47] Marissa Chen: We'll include webhook examples and a sample python snippet.
[10:51] Maya Gonzalez: Thanks all.
[10:53] Jordan Patel: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the doc pack by Monday.
[10:57] [crosstalk] Derek Shaw: Thanks. Bye.
[10:59] Jordan Patel: End meeting.

Notes on transcription quality: occasional mis-heard acronyms (KV cache transcribed as K V cash in some quick notes), product names sometimes show as "Redwood Optimise" in auto-captions. There is light crosstalk between Derek and Maya around 10:50.

Referenced artifacts/links in chat: [Eval API payload examples] (https://redwood.ai/docs/examples/eval-api-payloads), [SOC2 + security pack] (will be shared), [Pilot prompt-set template] (will be shared).

End of transcript.
